summary:
The Project Sirona is a website that permits teens, teachers, students, and even engineers to plan missions for a Lunar Landing. It's easy to understand interface was the team's aim : the already existing overlays can help for a first understanding and filter (slope, temperature, geology, ...), but engineers and other advanced user can add their own overlays.
Furthermore, we focused on a Role Play Game style, by drawing by hand every panel, adding a background music, and other RPG-like comparison features.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a 3D Moon in the web browser that helps mission planners find, compare and reach landing sites. It covers the conditions that matter most for a lander or a crewed base: sunlight for power, a radio link with Earth, temperature, slope, water and terrain. It has four modes:

  1. Visualisation. You can turn data layers on and off over the 3D Moon:
    Users can also add their own layer from any global PNG or GeoTIFF map of the Moon.
    • past space missions and noteworthy locations;
    • altitude, slope and terrain smoothness;
    • geology (from the USGS Unified Geologic Map) and water (H₂O);
    • surface temperature at any chosen date.
  2. Custom Point. Pick a latitude, a longitude and a date, and see where the Sun and the Earth are in the sky from that spot, over 1 to 366 days. It also gives the longest night and the longest time without a link to Earth. Hills and crater walls are taken into account, because they can hide the Sun or the Earth.
  3. Parametric Search. Describe the site you need with criteria such as “Sun visible more than 70 % of the time”, “Earth link gap shorter than 5 days”, “slope under 10°” or “near water”. You choose whether every criterion must hold or any one is enough, and whether it must hold for the whole period, on average, or at some point. The app finds the best areas, shows them on the Moon, lets you compare two of them side by side, and exports the results as a CSV file.
  4. Sirona Maps. Pick two points and a rover’s maximum slope. The app plans a route between them that avoids slopes steeper than the rover can climb, using an A* search on a high-resolution slope map.

The website sends its questions to our Python server. The server computes where the Sun and the Earth are with NASA’s SPICE toolkit and NASA NAIF data, and checks the relief with the LRO/LOLA elevation map. Temperatures come from the published 1-D thermal model of the lunar surface by Hayne et al. (2017).

Benefits

  • Many datasets in one place. Lighting, communications, temperature, terrain, water and geology are usually scattered across separate datasets and tools. Here they are on one interactive globe.
  • Answers to real planning questions. It answers “where” questions, like where a site meets all the conditions a mission needs, instead of only “what is here?”.
  • Relief and time are included. It looks at a site over a whole period and accounts for the terrain, which matters most near the poles, where the Sun stays low and craters cast long shadows.
  • The route matters too. It shows whether a rover can actually drive between two sites, not just whether each site is good on its own.
  • Easy to start. Anyone can run it with one click: the launcher installs everything and downloads the NASA data itself.

Intended impact

  • Make early landing-site studies faster and easier to share, for space agencies, students, researchers and the public, especially for the lunar south pole, where Artemis missions are heading.
  • Show clearly the trade-offs between power, communication, temperature and safety.
  • Help people understand the Moon as a real place to explore.

Tools, languages and data

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the website; Python for the server.
  • Website libraries: Three.js for the 3D rendering and geotiff.js for reading maps. There is no build step.
  • Server libraries: FastAPI and uvicorn for the server, SpiceyPy (NASA SPICE) for the Sun and Earth positions, NumPy, and tifffile with imagecodecs for the maps.
    • NASA’s CGI Moon Kit (LRO LROC colour map and LOLA elevation maps);
    • NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440 ephemeris, Moon orientation);
    • the USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon;
    • lunar water data;
    • a slope map computed from the LOLA elevation map;
    • a dataset of past lunar missions.
  • Hardware: our own laptops, nothing special. The app runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with Python and a web browser.

What makes it creative

  • It treats choosing a landing site as a search, not just a map you look at: you say what your mission needs, and the Moon shows you where those conditions are met.
  • It combines accurate orbital mechanics (SPICE), terrain shadowing, a thermal model and rover route planning in one simple interface.
  • It looks like a game, with side panels, tooltips, comparison cards and a soundtrack, but every number comes from NASA data and scientific models.
  • Users can add their own datasets as new layers, so the tool can grow with new data.

What our team considered

  • Scientific accuracy:
    • real ephemerides and Moon orientation;
    • correct map alignment, since a misaligned map gives every height and slope from the wrong place;
    • terrain hiding the Sun and the Earth;
    • stating the limits of our models clearly (for example, the temperature model assumes a smooth Moon).
  • What mission planners care about: power from sunlight, the longest night, gaps in the link with Earth, the temperature range, slope safety for landing and driving, and access to water.
  • Usability: a clean interface, a help page for each mode, the ability to compare and export results, and a one-click start for people who aren’t developers.
  • Speed and size: maps that are very large (gigabytes) are cut into tiles, read in pieces, or downloaded in the background, so the app stays responsive. Files too big for GitHub come straight from NASA instead.
  • Openness: it uses public NASA and USGS data and free open-source tools only, so anyone can check or reuse our work.
